title: Chapter 3.  History — British Annexation & the Anglo-Khasi War

blocks.content: The Anglo-Khasi War (1829-1833) is Meghalaya's most significant colonial-resistance episode, led by the Khasi chief U Tirot Sing - a figure now commemorated as one of North-East India's foremost early anti-colonial resistance leaders, predating the 1857 Revolt by decades.
Background: The Road Through the Khasi Hills

Following the British East India Company's acquisition of Assam (post the 1826 Treaty of Yandabo, covered in the companion Manipur GS volume's history chapters), the British sought to build a road through the Khasi Hills to connect the Bengal plains (Sylhet) with the newly acquired Assam region - a project requiring the cooperation of local Khasi chiefs, including U Tirot Sing, Syiem of the Hima Nongkhlaw.

U Tirot Sing initially permitted British road construction through his territory, but grew increasingly alarmed by the scale of British military and administrative encroachment associated with the project, ultimately withdrawing his cooperation and organising armed Khasi resistance against the British presence.

The resulting Anglo-Khasi War (1829-1833) saw U Tirot Sing lead a sustained guerrilla resistance campaign against British forces across the Khasi Hills' difficult terrain, for several years significantly disrupting British administrative and military control of the region before ultimately being defeated.

U Tirot Sing was eventually captured by British forces in 1833 and exiled to Dhaka (in present-day Bangladesh), where he died in captivity in 1835 - he is commemorated today as one of Meghalaya's foremost historical figures and a pioneering symbol of North-Eastern India's anti-colonial resistance, with his death anniversary (17 July) observed as U Tirot Sing Day, a Meghalaya state holiday.

Following the war's conclusion, the British gradually extended fuller administrative control across the Khasi, Jaintia and Garo Hills through the remainder of the 19th century, incorporating the region into British India's Assam administrative structure while, notably, maintaining certain distinct administrative arrangements for the hill tribal areas that would later influence the post-Independence Sixth Schedule framework (Chapter 5).
